title: Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co.
lead: A bank asks to close the books on a pooled trust fund, but its beneficiaries receive only a newspaper notice before their claims may be extinguished.

actors.name: Central Hanover Bank and Trust Company
actors.role: Trustee of the common fund seeking judicial settlement of its first account.

actors.name: Mullane
actors.role: Court-appointed special guardian and attorney for absent people with present or possible future income interests.

actors.name: Vaughan
actors.role: Court-appointed representative of principal interests; an appellee.

actors.name: The beneficiaries
actors.role: Holders of interests in participating trusts, some outside New York; none appeared personally.

proceedings: The Surrogate’s Court overruled Mullane’s notice objection and approved the account.
The Appellate Division and New York Court of Appeals affirmed.
The Supreme Court reversed and remanded because publication was inadequate for known present beneficiaries at known addresses.
limits: The ruling accepts publication for unknown or conjectural interests and does not require personal service or guarantee actual receipt by every beneficiary. No later accounting outcome is supplied.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Central Hanover pools small trusts in a common investment fund
sections.cue: What did pooling change, and why would a court accounting bind the beneficiaries?
paragraphs: New York Banking Law § 100-c allowed approved trust companies to combine assets of trusts they administered into a common investment fund. Each trust shared proportionately in income, gains, losses, and expenses, without owning any particular fund asset. The trust company alone managed the pool. Small trusts could thus gain diversification and economical management otherwise available mainly to larger trusts; the District of Columbia and about thirty states had similar arrangements.

The statute required a first court accounting twelve to fifteen months after the fund began and further accountings every three years. A decree settling an account conclusively bound everyone interested in the fund or its participating trusts on the matters disclosed. It could extinguish beneficiaries’ claims against the trustee for improper management during the covered period.

Central Hanover established its fund in January 1946. During the first accounting period, 113 trusts participated, about half created during life and half by wills, with nearly three million dollars in gross capital. Many beneficiaries held interests, and some lived outside New York. The record did not establish their number or residences.

sections.title: A newspaper announces the accounting, but names no beneficiary
sections.cue: What information had the trustee already mailed, and why was that different?
paragraphs: When each trust joined the fund, Central Hanover mailed a statutory notice to known beneficiaries of full age and sound mind entitled to income or, if the relevant event had occurred, principal. That mailing included provisions describing notice and judicial settlement. The bank had thus communicated directly with beneficiaries before any particular accounting came before a court.

In March 1947 the bank petitioned New York’s Surrogate’s Court, which handles estates and trusts, to settle its first account. For this proceeding, however, it used only the publication required by § 100-c(12): four successive weeks in a local newspaper. The notice gave the bank’s name and address, identified the fund and its establishment date, and listed participating trusts. It named no beneficiaries.

The court appointed Mullane as special guardian and attorney for absent persons, known or unknown, with present or possible future income interests. Vaughan represented principal interests. Such a guardian protects people absent or unable to act for themselves, but neither the bank nor the appointed guardian was required or apparently expected to warn the beneficiaries individually. Their property also bore the guardians’ fees and expenses. None of the beneficiaries themselves appeared.

sources.pinpoint: Parties; Material Facts; Reasoning; 339 U.S. at 309–11, 316

sections.title: Mullane contests the power to enter a binding decree
sections.cue: How did the notice objection reach the Supreme Court?
paragraphs: Mullane appeared specially, limiting his appearance to a challenge to the court’s authority rather than submitting to it. He argued that newspaper publication did not satisfy the Fourteenth Amendment and that the Surrogate therefore lacked jurisdiction to enter a final decree binding the absent beneficiaries.

The Surrogate overruled his objection and approved the account. The Appellate Division affirmed, and the New York Court of Appeals likewise held the notice constitutionally sufficient. Mullane appealed to the Supreme Court through the route then available when a state’s highest court sustained a state statute against federal constitutional attack. The Court heard argument on February 8, 1950.

sections.title: Jackson separates New York’s authority from the adequacy of its notice
sections.cue: Why did the old in-personam and in-rem labels not settle the case?
paragraphs: Justice Jackson wrote for the Supreme Court. Mullane first drew on Pennoyer: because the accounting resolved beneficiaries’ personal rights to surcharge the trustee rather than title or possession of particular property, he characterized it as an in-personam action that could not bind nonresidents lacking personal service within New York. An in-rem proceeding, by contrast, determines rights in a thing.

The Court declined to make the case turn on that classification. Fiduciary accountings had received several labels, this proceeding combined features of both categories, and intangible property had blurred distinctions inherited from a different property system. Fourteenth Amendment requirements could not depend on labels so elusive and variable among states. New York’s interest in closing trusts created under its laws and supervised by its courts justified determining all beneficiaries’ interests, wherever they lived, if they received a full opportunity to appear and be heard.

That proviso required a separate notice inquiry. The decree could destroy claims for negligent or unlawful impairment of the fund, and guardian fees could reduce interests through a contest conducted without the beneficiaries’ knowledge. Against the State’s vital interest in final settlement stood the beneficiaries’ opportunity to be heard, the interest emphasized in Grannis v. Ordean. A hearing opportunity means little when a person cannot learn that a matter is pending and decide whether to contest it.

sections.title: The Court asks how someone actually trying to inform these beneficiaries would act
sections.cue: What notice method fits the circumstances?
paragraphs: Personal delivery of written notice within the jurisdiction was the classic adequate method, but due process did not make it indispensable in every proceeding or impose impossible barriers to trust administration. The Court instead required notice reasonably calculated, in the circumstances, to disclose the pending action and afford an opportunity to object. It must convey the needed information and allow reasonable response time. The chosen means must resemble what a person actually trying to inform the absentee would reasonably use.

That standard has two branches: notice reasonably certain to inform, or, when circumstances do not reasonably permit that, a substitute not substantially less likely to succeed than feasible and customary alternatives. A mere gesture is insufficient. The inquiry evaluates the selected method in light of available knowledge, rather than demanding proof that everyone actually received notice.

A small newspaper advertisement depended on chance even for local residents and was still less likely to reach people outside the circulation area. Omitting beneficiary names also prevented acquaintances from recognizing whose rights were at stake. Publication sometimes supplements seizure of a ship or chattel or legal entry onto land, events likely to alert an owner or caretaker. Here, beneficiaries had not abandoned their interests, and the trustee ordinarily protecting them had become their adversary in seeking release from liability. That relationship supplied no equivalent warning.

sections.title: Unknown interests and known addresses lead to different answers
sections.cue: Why could publication suffice for some beneficiaries but fail for others?
paragraphs: For beneficiaries whose interests or whereabouts could not be discovered with due diligence, publication could suffice even if probably futile. Nothing substantially better was reasonably available. The Court likewise allowed publication for conjectural or future interests and for persons discoverable only through investigation whose interests had not become known in the ordinary course of administration. Constantly tracking changing income interests, presumed future holders of principal, and still more contingent interests could consume the advantages the pooling arrangement was designed to create. Due process did not require those searches.

Known present beneficiaries at known addresses were different. The bank had names and addresses in its records and regularly sent income payments. Once a practical, reliable way to communicate lay at hand, necessity no longer justified publication alone. Mailing statutory provisions months or years before the accounting did not inform them of this pending proceeding.

Ordinary mail would satisfy the practical need without requiring personal service. The bank’s earlier notices showed mailing would not seriously burden the fund. A prudent businessperson trying to convey information economically to people already listed in the files would not rely solely on an advertisement. Drawing on McDonald v. Mabee, the Court resisted letting legal fiction displace the facts needed for fair play.

The Court accepted a reasonable risk that not every beneficiary would actually receive notice. Each had the same interest in fund integrity and trustee fidelity, so a successful objection by one would benefit all. A method reasonably certain to reach most who might object could therefore protect the whole group. That explanation depends on the shared interests characteristic of this representative proceeding; it is not a general license to overlook individual notice in ordinary two-party suits. Personal service outside New York could also inform perfectly well even if it supplied no coercive jurisdiction, further illustrating why notice and adjudicatory power are distinct.

sections.title: The judgment rejects the known-beneficiary notice and leaves the other categories intact
sections.cue: What did Burton dispute, and what happened to the decree?
paragraphs: On April 24, 1950, the Supreme Court reversed the New York Court of Appeals and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion. It expressly rejected the constitutional objections asserted for beneficiaries whose interests or addresses were unknown to the trustee. The defect concerned substantial property rights of known present beneficiaries whose whereabouts were known and whom the bank could readily notify by mail. Failure to reach every individual was not itself the constitutional flaw; choosing a poorly calculated method when a feasible superior one existed was.

Justice Burton dissented. He stressed that participating trust instruments had to permit entry into a common fund and regarded any additional notice beyond New York’s publication and representation safeguards as a matter for the State’s discretion. He did not believe the Federal Constitution required more. The casebook omits that dissent, but the reviewed full brief includes it. Justice Douglas did not participate.

Mullane’s distinction between power and notice means that a court with jurisdiction can still violate due process through defective notice. Its reduced reliance on in-rem labels also anticipates, without itself announcing, Shaffer’s later minimum-contacts treatment of all state-court jurisdiction. Its attention to the individual interest and cost of better procedures anticipates Mathews balancing. In the later Eisen decision, 417 U.S. 156 (1974), the Court used Mullane when requiring individual notice to Rule 23(b)(3) class members identifiable through reasonable effort. Those later decisions are doctrinal developments, not further stages of Central Hanover’s accounting.
